title: Docker Containerization
description: Package your ASP.NET Core application into a Docker container for consistent, repeatable deployments across any environment. Learn multi-stage Dockerfiles, container image optimization, and how to run and manage containers in development and production.

blocks.text: Docker containers package an application and all its dependencies — runtime, libraries, configuration, and code — into a single, portable image. The same container image that runs on your development machine runs identically in production, eliminating the 'it works on my machine' problem that plagues traditional deployments.

ASP.NET Core is an excellent fit for containers because it is cross-platform, has a small footprint, and supports multi-stage Docker builds that keep final images lean. A production-ready ASP.NET Core Docker image can be under 200MB, compared to over 1GB for a traditional server installation.

A Docker image is a read-only template containing your application code, the .NET runtime, and any system-level dependencies. A Docker container is a running instance of an image. Multiple containers can run from the same image, each isolated from the others. Images are versioned and stored in registries like Docker Hub or Azure Container Registry.

Think of a Docker image as a blueprint and a container as a house built from that blueprint. You can build an image once and run as many containers as you need from it. If you update the application, you build a new image version. Containers from the old image continue running until you replace them.

Docker images are built in layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer. Docker caches each layer, so if only your application code changed but the base image and dependency restore step did not, Docker reuses the cached layers. This makes subsequent builds dramatically faster.

blocks.title: Order Your Dockerfile for Cache Efficiency
blocks.text: Put instructions that change rarely (base image, dependency restore) first. Put instructions that change often (copying source code) last. This maximizes Docker layer caching and keeps build times short.

Multi-stage builds are the key to keeping Docker images small. The build stage uses the full .NET SDK image to compile and publish your application. The runtime stage uses the much smaller ASP.NET runtime image and copies only the published output from the build stage. The SDK image — hundreds of megabytes — never appears in the final image.

blocks.title: Optimized Multi-Stage Dockerfile for ASP.NET Core
blocks.content: A production-ready Dockerfile using multi-stage builds to create a minimal runtime image.
blocks.code:
# Stage 1: Build — uses the full SDK image
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src

# Copy project file and restore dependencies (cached layer)
COPY ["MyApp.csproj", "./"]
RUN dotnet restore "./MyApp.csproj"

# Copy remaining source and build
COPY . .
RUN dotnet build -c Release -o /app/build

# Publish the app
RUN dotnet publish -c Release -o /app/publish /p:UseAppHost=false

# Stage 2: Runtime — uses the minimal runtime image
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app

# Create a non-root user for security
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S appgroup && \
    adduser -u 1001 -S appuser -G appgroup

# Copy published output from the build stage
COPY --from=build /app/publish .

# Set ownership and switch to non-root user
RUN chown -R appuser:appgroup /app
USER appuser

# Expose the application port
EXPOSE 8080

# Set environment variables
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
ENV ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production

# Start the application
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "MyApp.dll"]

blocks.text: Smaller images deploy faster, download faster, and use less disk space. Several techniques reduce image size: use the Alpine Linux variant of the runtime image, set UseAppHost=false during publish to avoid embedding a native executable, and use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files from the build context.

blocks.title: .dockerignore File for ASP.NET Core Projects
blocks.content: A .dockerignore file that excludes build artifacts, git files, and IDE configurations from the Docker build context.
blocks.code:
# Build artifacts
bin/
obj/

# IDE files
.vscode/
.idea/
*.user
*.suo
*.sln.docstates

# Git
git
gitignore
.git/
.gitattributes

# Docker files
Dockerfile
.dockerignore

# Test and docs (not needed in runtime image)
tests/
**/*.Tests.csproj
docs/
README.md

# npm / node (if frontend assets are pre-built)
node_modules/
wwwroot/dist/  # if pre-built locally, rebuild in container instead

blocks.text: Once you have built an image, you run it as a container. Docker run creates a new container from the image. You can map ports from the host to the container, mount volumes for persistent data, set environment variables, and control resource limits. In development, Docker Compose simplifies running multiple containers — your API, database, and Redis together.

blocks.title: Building and Running the Container
blocks.content: Commands to build the Docker image and run it as a container with port mapping and environment variables.
blocks.code:
# Build the Docker image and tag it
 docker build -t myapp:latest .

# Run the container, mapping port 8080 on the host to 8080 in the container
docker run --rm -d \
  --name myapp \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production" \
  -e "ConnectionStrings__Default=..." \
  myapp:latest

# Check the container is running
docker ps

# View the container logs
docker logs myapp

# Stop and remove the container
docker stop myapp && docker rm myapp

blocks.text: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications with a single YAML file. You can define your API container, a SQL Server container, and a Redis container together, with shared networks and volumes. This is the standard way to run a complete development environment with Docker.

blocks.title: Docker Compose for ASP.NET Core + SQL Server
blocks.content: A docker-compose.yml file defining an API service and a SQL Server database service.
blocks.code:
version: '3.8'

services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: MyApp/Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      - ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development
      - ConnectionStrings__Default=Server=db;Database=MyAppDb;User Id=sa;Password=YourStrong@Passw0rd;
    depends_on:
      - db
    volumes:
      - ./MyApp:/app  # Live-reload source code during development

  db:
    image: mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest
    environment:
      - SA_PASSWORD=YourStrong@Passw0rd
      - ACCEPT_EULA=Y
    ports:
      - "1433:1433"
    volumes:
      - sqldata:/var/opt/mssql

volumes:
  sqldata:

terms.definition: A read-only template containing an application, its runtime, and dependencies. Built from a Dockerfile.
A running instance of a Docker image — an isolated process with its own filesystem, network, and resources.
A Dockerfile technique using multiple FROM statements to compile in one image and copy only the output to a minimal runtime image.
An immutable filesystem layer in a Docker image. Docker caches layers to speed up rebuilds when earlier instructions have not changed.
A tool for defining and running multi-container applications using a YAML configuration file.

blocks.title: Use Non-Root Users in Containers
blocks.text: Running your application as a non-root user inside the container is a security best practice. The official ASP.NET Core Alpine images support creating and switching to a non-root user in your Dockerfile. This limits the blast radius if your application is compromised.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: Docker Containerization
points: Docker images package an application and its dependencies into a portable, versioned artifact
Multi-stage Docker builds separate the build stage (full SDK) from the runtime stage (minimal runtime image)
Layer caching makes subsequent Docker builds fast when source code has not changed
The Alpine Linux variant of the ASP.NET runtime image produces the smallest possible production images
.dockerignore prevents unnecessary files from being included in the Docker build context
Docker Compose defines multi-service applications — API, database, cache — in a single YAML file
blocks.takeaway: Docker containers make deployment consistent from development to production. A multi-stage Dockerfile with the Alpine runtime image gives you a small, secure, and fast-to-deploy artifact that runs identically everywhere. Combine it with Docker Compose for a complete local development environment.

blocks.title: Exercise: Create a Production-Ready Dockerfile
blocks.description: Write an optimized multi-stage Dockerfile for an ASP.NET Core API and test it locally.
steps: Create a .dockerignore file excluding bin/, obj/, .git/, .vscode/, and test projects
Create a multi-stage Dockerfile with a build stage using mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0-alpine
Add a non-root user in the runtime stage and set USER to that user
Set ASPNETCORE_URLS and ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT environment variables in the runtime stage
Build the image with docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
Run the container with docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0 and confirm it responds
blocks.expectedOutcome: A working Dockerfile that builds an image under 200MB, runs as a non-root user, and serves the API on port 8080. The container responds correctly to HTTP requests, and the build completes without warnings.

items.text: I can explain what a Docker image and container are
items.hint: Image = blueprint/template. Container = running instance of an image.

items.text: I understand why multi-stage builds produce smaller images
items.hint: The SDK (large) is only in the build stage. The runtime (small) is the only thing in the final image.

items.text: I know why Dockerfile instruction order matters for caching
items.hint: Instructions that rarely change go first. Instructions that change often (COPY . .) go last.

items.text: I can write a .dockerignore file to speed up builds
items.hint: Exclude bin/, obj/, .git/, IDE files, and anything not needed at runtime.

items.text: I understand why running as a non-root user in containers is a security best practice
items.hint: If the app is compromised, a non-root user limits the attacker's ability to damage the container or host.
